analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their spouses from owning or trading individual stocks.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan ban on congressional stock ownership was introduced in February 2022 with five cosponsors but never received a vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have prohibited sitting members of Congress and their spouses from owning or trading stocks, bonds, commodities, futures, and other securities, including hedge fund and private equity stakes, to prevent lawmakers from profiting off information they gain from writing laws. Members would have had 180 days to divest (five years for complex private investments), with exceptions for diversified mutual funds, Treasury securities, government retirement plans, and certain small business holdings. Violations could draw civil fines of up to $50,000 per violation enforced by the Attorney General or Special Counsel. The bill was introduced in the Senate in February 2022 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, but never advanced to a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday Americans who want to be sure their elected representatives aren't trading on inside information about legislation or regulatory decisions. The bill would remove the financial incentive for members of Congress to use their positions to benefit their own investment portfolios, and would prevent spouses from trading on insider knowledge. Investors in general could benefit from reduced perception of congressional insider trading.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary Americans and financial market integrity

how_it_helps.text: Would prohibit sitting members of Congress and their spouses from owning or trading stocks, bonds, commodities, futures, and other securities [S2][S3].

Members and spouses would have 180 days to divest, or five years for hedge fund and venture capital holdings, with exceptions for diversified mutual funds, Treasury securities, and government retirement plans [S2][S3].
Violations would carry civil fines of up to $50,000 per violation, enforceable by the Attorney General or Special Counsel [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their spouses, who would have to divest potentially substantial stock holdings and give up the ability to profit from securities markets while holding office. Wealthy members with complex investment portfolios would face the biggest adjustment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their spouses

drawbacks.text: The $50,000 civil fine cap per violation is small relative to the wealth of many members of Congress and the size of trades that could be made, potentially an insufficient deterrent [S3].
Members could still own diversified mutual funds and retirement plans, meaning they would still have broad market exposure, though without direct trading authority or single-company stakes [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and well-documented concern: that lawmakers can profit from information only they have access to. The cost is borne only by a small group of officials, not the general public. Its principal weakness is a fine structure too modest to deter well-off members, and it exempts diversified funds, which limits but does not eliminate all conflict-of-interest concerns.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the Senate and referred to the Finance Committee, but it never got a vote and expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on February 10, 2022, with five cosponsors [S1][S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the same day, where it stalled [S1][S5].
The Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee held a hearing related to the issue in April 2022, but the bill never advanced to the floor [S5].
No further action was recorded, and the bill died at the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress who want to keep trading individual stocks and owning securities benefited from the bill never advancing, since they retain the current disclosure-only regime under existing law.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban congressional stock ownership and trading.

for.name: Sen. Mike Daines, Marsha Blackburn, Debbie Stabenow, Raphael Warnock, and Lindsey Graham
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee markup or vote after referral, letting it sit until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship from three Republicans and two Democrats, but it never reached a vote, so actual party-line support or opposition was never tested.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their households
industries.note: The bill would directly eliminate their ability to own and trade securities while in office, ending a financial privilege available to few other professions with similar access to nonpublic information.
